problem: Given that the polynomial $f(x)=5{x}^{3}+35{x}^{2}+2x+14$ has a root in the interval $(-15,-6),$ find the sum of the **distinct** real roots of $f(x).$

feedback.problem: Given that the polynomial $f(x)=8{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}-2x+1$ has a root in the interval $(\frac{1}{4},1),$ find the sum of the **distinct** real roots of $f(x).$
feedback.worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $1$ and the leading coefficient is $8.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }1}{\text{factor of }8}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm \frac{1}{8},\,\pm \frac{1}{4},\,\pm \frac{1}{2},\,\pm 1
$$

Of these roots, the only root in the interval $(\frac{1}{4},1)$ is $\frac{1}{2}.$

Using the synthetic division, we get the following:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\frac{1}{2}$ | $8$ | $-4$ | $-2$ | $1$ |
|  | $↓$ | $4$ | $0$ | $-1$ |
|  | $8$ | $0$ | $-2$ | $0$ |

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x-\frac{1}{2})(8{x}^{2}-2).\end{aligned}
$$

Since the highest-degree factor is now a quadratic, we can continue factoring using the usual methods:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x-\frac{1}{2})(8{x}^{2}-2) \\  & =2(x-\frac{1}{2})(4{x}^{2}-1) \\  & =(2x-1)(2x+1)(2x-1) \\  & =(2x+1)(2x-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the factors equal to $0,$ we find the roots $x=-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}.$ Summing these roots, we get

$$
-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=0.
$$
